questions.stem:
Choose the correct sentence:
A. He is one of the few persons who believes in hard work.
B. He is one of the few persons who believe in hard work.

options.option_text: A
B
Both are equally correct
Neither is correct

questions.explanation: B is correct. In 'one of the... who...' construction: the verb in the relative clause agrees with the plural noun, not with 'one.' 'He is one of the few persons WHO BELIEVE (plural).' Exception: 'He is the only one who BELIEVES (singular)' — 'only' makes it singular.

options.option_text: She spoke very highly for you.
She spoke very highly of you.
She spoke very highly about you.
She highly spoke of you.

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'SPEAK HIGHLY OF someone' is the fixed phrase. Other collocation patterns: think highly OF, speak ill OF, speak well OF. The preposition 'of' is fixed in this expression.

questions.stem: Identify the correct sentence regarding 'would rather':

options.option_text: I would rather to go home now.
I would rather go home now.
I would rather going home now.
I would rather have to go home now.

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'WOULD RATHER + base verb (bare infinitive, no 'to').' 'I would rather GO home' ✓. Never: 'would rather TO go' or 'would rather going.' Also: 'Would rather + past subjunctive' for preferences about others: 'I would rather you STAYED.'

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence regarding 'used to':

options.option_text: He use to play cricket.
He is used to playing cricket.
He used to play cricket when he was young.
He is used to play cricket.

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'USED TO + base verb' = past habit (no longer done). 'He USED TO PLAY cricket' = he regularly played before but doesn't now. 'BE USED TO + gerund' = accustomed to: 'He IS USED TO PLAYING cricket' = he is accustomed to it (possibly still plays). These are different structures.

options.option_text: The cattle is grazing in the field.
The cattle are grazing in the field.
The cattles are grazing in the field.
The cattle was grazing in the field.

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'CATTLE' = always plural; no singular form (one cow, not 'one cattle'). 'The cattle ARE grazing' ✓. Similarly always-plural: police, people, gentry, nobility, clergy. These collective nouns take plural verbs.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct use of 'lest':
A. He ran fast lest he should miss the train.
B. He ran fast lest he should not miss the train.
C. He ran fast lest he will miss the train.
D. He ran fast lest he would miss the train.

options.option_text: B
A
C
D

questions.explanation: B is correct (Option A in the question). 'LEST + should + V1' = for fear that. 'He ran fast LEST HE SHOULD MISS the train' = he ran for fear of missing the train. Key rules: (1) 'lest' is always followed by 'should'; (2) NEVER add 'not' after 'lest' (lest already implies negative purpose).

options.option_text: She wears this dress since Monday.
She has been wearing this dress since Monday.
She wore this dress since Monday.
She is wearing this dress since Monday.

questions.explanation: B is correct. SINCE + point in time → use PRESENT PERFECT or PRESENT PERFECT CONTINUOUS. 'She HAS BEEN WEARING this dress since Monday' = started wearing on Monday, still wearing now. 'She wore' (simple past) would imply the action is complete.

questions.stem: Choose the grammatically correct sentence involving 'scarcely':

options.option_text: He had scarcely left than the phone rang.
Scarcely he had left when the phone rang.
Scarcely had he left when the phone rang.
He had scarcely left but the phone rang.

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'SCARCELY...WHEN' = barely/almost not before something else happened. When 'scarcely' is at the beginning: INVERSION: 'Scarcely HAD HE left WHEN...' Similar: HARDLY...WHEN; NO SOONER...THAN. All negative time adverbs at sentence start require subject-auxiliary inversion.

options.option_text: The accused pleaded not guilty.
The accused pleaded as not guilty.
The accused pleaded not guilty to.
The accused was pleaded not guilty.

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'PLEAD NOT GUILTY' or 'PLEAD GUILTY' is the standard legal/formal expression. No preposition after 'plead' in this usage. 'The accused pleaded NOT GUILTY to the charges' (when 'to the charges' follows, it's also standard). Without 'to', option A is perfectly correct.

questions.stem: Choose the grammatically correct sentence regarding countable/uncountable nouns:

options.option_text: Can you give me an information?
Can you give me some information?
Can you give me informations?
Can you give me the informations?

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'INFORMATION' is UNCOUNTABLE and has no plural form. Use 'some information,' 'a piece of information,' 'this information.' Never 'an information' or 'informations.' Other always-uncountable nouns: advice, furniture, luggage, equipment, news, knowledge, scenery.
